figure: Figure 15.2, left panel (a) 'Caching removes prefill work'

figure: Figure 15.2, left panel ('Caching removes prefill work')
issue: The y-axis is labeled 'Prefill FLOPs / req' and the plotted formula f(r)=(S+P/r)/(S+P) treats prefill cost as linear in token counts. Prefill FLOPs are not linear in sequence length because attention contributes a quadratic term and because per-layer/fixed costs do not scale exactly with token count. The caption calls the curves illustrative but does not state the linear-cost assumption, so the figure can be read as a FLOPs model rather than a simplified token-work model.
evidence: Axis label: 'Prefill FLOPs / req (% of no-cache)'; formula: 'f(r)=(S+P/r)/(S+P)' with 'P=40%, S=60%'; caption: 'illustrative (synthetic) curves, not measured benchmarks' but no linear-cost caveat.
acceptance_test: Either relabel the y-axis to 'Relative prefill token-work (linear-cost model)' and add the linear-cost assumption to the caption/formula, or replace the formula with a cost model that includes the attention quadratic term and state the model's scope. The figure must not imply that prefill FLOPs are exactly linear in prefix/suffix length.

figure: FIGURE 15.2(a) — Prefill work vs average prefix reuse
issue: The y-axis label "Prefill FLOPs / req (M)" contradicts the caption, which describes the same quantity as "as a percent of no-cache prefill." Read literally, the axis asserts that a no-cache request costs 100 MFLOPs of prefill. That is off by roughly six orders of magnitude from any real LLM (the canonical 1,200-token prefill on a 70B model is ~1.7×10^14 FLOPs, i.e. ~168 TFLOPs, not 100 MFLOPs). A reader who quotes the axis as an absolute figure will be wrong by a factor of ~10^6; a reader who reads the caption will be right. The figure and its caption currently describe two different quantities.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 259: y-axis reads "Prefill FLOPs / req (M)" with ticks 0–100 and the "no cache" series flat at exactly 100. Caption: "(left: prefill work vs average prefix reuse, as a percent of no-cache prefill, lower is better ...)". The two readings are mutually exclusive: 100 MFLOPs/req is not 100% of no-cache prefill for any model in the book.
acceptance_test: Choose one quantity and make axis and caption agree. Preferred: relabel the axis "Prefill work per request (% of no-cache)" (or "Prefill FLOPs / req (relative; no-cache = 100)") and delete the "(M)". Re-render and confirm no absolute FLOP unit appears on this axis, and that the caption's "percent of no-cache prefill" matches the axis text verbatim.

figure: FIGURE 15.2(a) — Prefill work vs average prefix reuse (in-figure annotation)
issue: The figure's own parameters are undefined and insufficient to reproduce the curve. The annotation reads "f(r)=5/(1+r); P=40%, S=60%" but the caption never defines P or S, and the plotted curve is not f(r) — it is 100·[S + P·f(r)/f(1)], i.e. 60 + 80/(1+r). The normalization by f(1)=2.5 and the combination rule are both unstated, so a reader who tries to reproduce the curve from the annotation gets 5/(1+r) and cannot match the drawing. The reader also cannot tell why the curve floors at ~60 rather than 0 (the S=60% non-cacheable share of prefill), which is the single most decision-relevant feature of the curve.
evidence: Rendered page, PDF 259: annotation "f(r)=5/(1+r); P=40%, S=60%". Caption describes only the axes and the meaning of "average prefix reuse"; it never mentions P, S, or f. Recomputation against the drawn curve: 100·[0.6 + 0.4·(5/(1+r))/(5/2)] = 60 + 80/(1+r) gives r=1→100, r=2→86.7, r=3→80, r=5→73.3, r=10→67.3, r=100→60.8, matching the drawn green curve (which flattens at ~60). The unnormalized f(r)=5/(1+r) would give 2.5 at r=1 and 0.05 at r=100, which does not match.
acceptance_test: Either (a) put the full formula in the figure annotation, e.g. "prefill work = S + P·f(r)/f(1); f(r)=5/(1+r), f(1)=2.5; P=40% cacheable, S=60% not cacheable", or (b) move the formula into the caption and define P and S there in words. Acceptance: a reader with only the figure and its caption can state what P and S mean, can reproduce the curve at r=1, 10 and 100, and can explain the ~60% floor.
